note_claims.claim: Right-sided sciatica-type leg pain for 3 weeks.
Onset occurred 3 weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Pain radiates from the buttock down the posterior thigh and lateral calf into the foot.
Pain is worse than back pain.
Pain is up to 7/10 and is worse after sitting.
Occasional tingling is present over the lateral foot.
No weakness is present.
No saddle anaesthesia or change in bladder or bowel function is present.
No fevers are present.
No history of cancer or unintentional weight loss is present.
Over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily is being taken with little benefit.
No other medications are being taken.
No known drug allergies are present.
No history of peptic ulcer, asthma, or renal disease is present.
Lumbar flexion is limited by pain.
Straight leg raise is positive on the left at 40 degrees.
Power, reflexes, and sensation are normal and symmetrical in both lower limbs.
Impression is right-sided sciatica, likely lumbar disc-related radiculopathy.
Plan is to stop ibuprofen and start naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food and omeprazole 20 mg once daily for 2 weeks.
Plan includes referral to physiotherapy.
Patient is advised to keep active and avoid bed rest.
A fit note for two weeks is provided, allowing the patient to be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
Follow-up is scheduled in four weeks.
A symptom card is given to the patient.

transcript_facts.fact: Patient reports the complaint is 'my back' and 'my leg, really' with 'shooting pain going all the way down'.
The pain started about three weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Patient is a care assistant at a nursing home.
The pain is definitely in the right leg, despite the patient saying they always mix them up.
The pain goes from the bum, down the back of the thigh, round the outside of the calf, and into the foot.
The pain is seven on a bad day and is worse when sitting for a while.
The patient confirms the leg is worse than the back.
The patient experiences a bit of tingling on the outside of their foot sometimes.
The patient reports no weakness, only pain.
Patient denies numbness around the bottom or between legs when sitting on the toilet.
Patient reports no change in waterworks (trouble passing urine or leaking).
Patient reports no problems with bowels or accidents.
Patient reports no fevers or feeling unwell.
Patient denies having ever had cancer or lost weight without trying.
Patient is taking Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day, which 'barely touches it'.
Patient reports no other medicines and no allergies.
When the clinician lifts the right leg straight, the patient reports pain that 'shoots right down'.
The clinician notes the pain is at about 40 degrees when the right leg is lifted.
The left leg is fine when lifted.
The clinician notes that power, knee and ankle reflexes are normal in both legs.
The patient confirms they can feel the clinician touching both sides.
The clinician suggests the finding sounds like sciatica, where a disc in the lower back is irritating a nerve going down the right leg.
The clinician plans to switch the patient from ibuprofen to naproxen 500 milligrams twice a day with food and add omeprazole 20 milligrams once a day for a couple of weeks.
The clinician plans to refer the patient to physiotherapy.
The clinician plans to give a fit note for two weeks, stating the patient may be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
The clinician plans to review the patient in four weeks.

The clinician provides safety-netting advice: if the patient gets numbness around the bottom or genitals, difficulty passing urine, loss of control of bladder or bowels, or weakness in both legs, they should go to A&E straight away due to the risk of cauda equina syndrome.
